An **amplifier** makes a small signal big enough to move a speaker. Instrument amps are part of the instrument's
sound; a **PA** (public address) should just make everything louder, faithfully.

## Instrument amps

- **Combo** (amp and speaker in one box) or **head and cabinet**.
- The usual controls: **Gain** (or Drive) sets how hard the preamp is pushed: low is clean, high distorts.
  **Volume / Master** sets how loud. **Bass, Mid, Treble** shape it; **Presence** adds upper bite.
- **Guitar amps** colour the sound heavily and are meant to. **Bass amps** need much more power for the same
  loudness (low notes take more energy), and are built to stay clean and reach low. **Keyboard amps** are flatter,
  more like a small PA. (More below: [Guitar amps and bass amps](#guitar-amps-and-bass-amps).)
- Start everything at noon (12 o'clock), gain low, then adjust. Small changes.
- Valve (tube) amps need a minute to warm up and should go into **standby** for breaks. Never run one without a
  speaker connected: it can destroy the output transformer.
- **Impedance** (ohms) of the cabinet must match what the head expects (printed by the speaker jack).

### Gain (or Volume) and Master: two volume knobs

An amp is two amplifiers in a row. The **preamp** takes the tiny signal from the guitar and shapes it; the **power
amp** makes it strong enough to drive the speaker. Each knob sits in front of one of them:

- **Gain**, **Drive**, or on many amps a knob just called **Volume** (sometimes per channel), sets how hard the
  signal hits the preamp. That decides the **sound**: low is clean, higher breaks up, highest is full distortion.
  It changes loudness too, but only until the preamp is clipping; after that more gain means more distortion, not more level.
- **Master** sits between the preamp and the power amp and decides **how loud** all of that is in the room. It
  doesn't change the character, so you can have a fully distorted sound quietly at home, or a clean one loud.

Set them in that order: Master low, Gain for the sound you want, then Master up to the level the room needs. It's
the same idea as [gain staging](rec-gain-staging.qmd) on a mixer: the first knob sets the sound, the last one the loudness.

An old-style amp with **only one Volume** (many vintage Fenders and Voxes) has no master: the one knob does both,
so it is clean when quiet and only starts to break up when it is loud. That's why those amps are "too loud" to get
their overdrive at home. On a valve amp, turning the Master far up drives the **power valves** too, which adds a
second, looser kind of distortion that a low-master setting can't give you.

### Treble and Presence

Both turn up the high end, and on a lot of amps they sit side by side, so they look like the same knob twice.
They aren't. **Presence** is a treble control, but not a second Treble knob. It works on a higher band (roughly 2–6 kHz:
pick attack, string edge, the "cut" that lets a guitar be heard through a band), and it sits in a different place:

- **Treble** is in the preamp's tone stack, **before** or in the middle of the distortion. Turning it up also
  changes what gets distorted, and so how the distortion sounds.
- **Presence** is in the **power amp**, **after** the distortion. On a valve amp it reduces the power amp's
  negative feedback at high frequencies (the circuit that keeps the power amp flat), so those frequencies come
  through stronger. On a solid-state or modelling amp it's a high-frequency boost placed at the same point. It
  adds clarity without changing how the drive feels.

Too little and the amp sounds woolly and lost in the mix, even when it's loud. Too much sounds harsh and fizzy
(the "ice pick", worst with high gain and in small rooms). Start it at noon, set Treble first, then use Presence to
make the guitar cut through the band. Some amps have a matching low control, **Resonance** or **Depth**, which
does the same thing for the low end. On a bass amp the equivalent (sometimes **Bright**) helps slap and fingernoise speak.

| | **Treble** | **Presence** |
|---|---|---|
| Where | preamp tone stack, before the power amp | power amp, after the distortion |
| Range | a shelf from about 2.5 kHz up (everything above) | a broad bump around 2–6 kHz |
| With distortion | changes what gets distorted: more treble in, a buzzier, tighter drive | brightens the distortion that's already there, like EQ after it |
| Too much | thin, spiky | harsh, fizzy, "ice pick" |
| Use it for | the basic colour of the sound | cutting through a band without more gain |

To hear it, set **High gain, quiet**, then turn **Treble** from 3 to 8: the distortion itself changes, getting
buzzier and tighter. Back to 5, and turn **Presence** from 3 to 8 instead: the same distortion, just brighter on top.

### Middle and the Mid frequency

The **Middle** knob boosts or cuts one band, and where that band sits matters as much as how much. On most guitar amps it is
fixed, somewhere around 500 Hz to 800 Hz. Many bass amps and some guitar amps (and almost every mixer channel, see the
[mixer](#try-it-one-channel)) let you move it with a second knob, **Mid frequency** (a "sweepable" or semi-parametric mid):

- **200–400 Hz**: body and boom. Cut here when the guitar is muddy or fights the bass; boost on a thin bass.
- **500 Hz–1 kHz**: the honk and growl. A guitar's mids live here; so does the "growl" of a bass that cuts through.
- **1.5–3 kHz**: bite, pick and finger attack. Boost for a bass that has to be heard on small speakers.

To find a frequency: boost the Middle a lot (8 or 9), sweep the Mid frequency until it sounds worst (or best),
then set the Middle back to the amount you want. The **scooped** sound (Middle at 2 or 3, bass and treble up) is
big and exciting alone, and disappears as soon as the band plays, because the middle is where a guitar is heard.

### Guitar amps and bass amps

A bass's low E is 41 Hz; a guitar's is 82 Hz. Most of the differences follow from that octave:

- **Power.** Moving the air for low notes takes far more energy: a bass amp needs several times the watts of a guitar amp
  to keep up with it (300–500 W against a 30–50 W guitar valve amp in a band).
- **Clean on purpose.** A guitar amp is designed to distort when pushed. A bass amp is designed to stay clean (more
  headroom, in the simulation: the same Gain distorts later); bass drive is something added on purpose, gently,
  usually keeping the clean lows underneath (**Bass, growl**).
- **The EQ sits lower.** Bass at about 40–60 Hz instead of 100 Hz, a mid that is often sweepable, treble at 4–5 kHz
  and up for string and slap noise. Many bass amps add a graphic EQ.
- **The cabinet goes deeper and is closed**, often with a **horn tweeter** for the top (see Cabinets below).
- **A DI out.** Bass amps nearly always have an XLR **DI output**, so the PA gets the bass directly while the amp is
  only for the stage.

Playing bass through a guitar amp works quietly, but the amp throws away the bottom octave (the low-cut at the input
and the cabinet's roll-off), and loud low notes can tear a guitar speaker, which isn't built to move that far.
Try **Bass through a guitar amp**, then **Bass amp**. A guitar through a bass amp is safe, just clean and polite.

### Cabinets

The speaker cabinet is the last, and largest, tone control. The amp's raw output is harsh and fizzy (pick
**No cabinet** to hear it); the speakers roll off almost everything above 5 kHz, and that roll-off is a large part of what
"guitar tone" is. This is also why recording a guitar amp means a mic on a speaker, or a cabinet simulation (an **IR**,
impulse response) when there is no speaker. What decides a cabinet's sound:

- **Speaker size.** A smaller cone moves faster and reaches higher but goes less deep: **10″** speakers sound quick, bright
  and punchy; **12″** is the usual guitar speaker, fuller, rolling off around 5 kHz; **15″** goes deep and round and has
  almost no top (old-school bass).
- **How many.** More speakers move more air: louder, and fuller at the bottom, at the same amp power. They also
  interfere with each other a little (a dip in the upper mids, which changes where you stand) and spread the sound
  more narrowly. A **4×10** and a **2×12** have roughly the same cone area but sound different: the 4×10 tighter and brighter, the 2×12 warmer.
- **Open or closed back.** An **open-back** combo also radiates from the back, and the back wave cancels the front's
  lowest notes: airy, spread out, less bass, fills a room. A **closed-back** cabinet (most 4×12s and nearly all bass
  cabinets) traps that air: tight, punchy low end with a thump around 100 Hz, and more directional (beamy).
- **A horn tweeter** (bass cabinets): a small extra speaker that adds back the top end that big cones can't make, with
  a level knob or switch on the back. Turn it down for an old-school sound.
- **Impedance and power handling** must match the amp (printed on the back, see above).

In the simulation, the cabinet changes the low end, the upper mids and the roll-off; switch between **2×12 open back** and
**4×10 open back** on the same setting, or **4×12 closed back** with high gain. It can't model the real differences in
loudness, spread and how a cab interacts with the room, but you can hear the colour.

### Try it

Start with **Clean**, then **Crunch**: the Gain moved (and the cabinet is a 2×12). **High gain, quiet** is a full distortion at a low
Master; **Clean, loud** is the opposite. **Vintage, cranked** greys out the Master: the one Volume knob makes it
dirty and loud together. Then sweep **Presence** from 0 to 10 with the Treble left alone. Play your own notes from
the keys at the foot of the page, or plug in a guitar (Source: Microphone, through an audio interface; headphones on).
The guitar and bass riffs are the band's own recorded samples, unamplified, as if the instrument were plugged
straight into a desk. **Bass amp**, **Bass, growl** and **Bass through a guitar amp** switch the source to the bass riff.
**View** switches the controls between sliders and knobs; click any number to type a value.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Modelling amps: the knobs may be lying

Many small practice amps are **modelling amps**: a computer that imitates many amps and stores **presets**. The
**Fender Mustang** series, Boss Katana, Line 6 Spider, Positive Grid Spark and Yamaha THR are all like this. When
you choose a preset (or switch the amp on, which loads one), the amp uses the preset's stored Gain, Volume and EQ,
**not** what the physical knobs point at. A Volume knob sitting at 2 can be playing a preset saved at 10. Turn
a knob and the setting jumps to where the knob is.

So:

1. Before switching on and before changing presets, turn **Master to 1** (on amps where Master is the one real,
   unstored knob, as on the Mustangs, it is the one control you can trust).
2. Choose the preset, play, and bring the Master up slowly to the level you want.
3. Then touch the other knobs one at a time to take control of them, and **save** if you want to keep the result.
:::

## Powered and passive speakers

- **Powered (active)**: the amplifier is inside. Plug in power and a line-level signal. Most small PAs and studio
  monitors.
- **Passive**: needs a separate power amp and speaker cable. Never plug a passive speaker into a line output, or a
  speaker output into a line input.

## A small PA

A typical small rig: mics and instruments → **mixer** → two powered speakers on stands (the **mains**), plus
**monitor** wedges for the players.

On each mixer channel, top to bottom:

1. **Gain / Trim**: set this first. Play or sing at full performance level and turn up until the peak light only
   just flickers, or the meter sits around 0 to −6. ([Recording 1](rec-gain-staging.qmd))
2. **High-pass (low cut)** on for vocals and anything without real bass.
3. **EQ**: small cuts, not big boosts.
4. **Aux sends**: the monitor mixes (pre-fader) and effects (post-fader).
5. **Pan**, **Mute**, and the **fader**, near 0 for the main sound.

### Try it: one channel

Press **Start here**, then work down the strip in the lesson's order. Bring the **Gain** up while the singer sings
until the After-gain meter sits near the dashed line and PEAK only flickers, switch the **High-pass** on, then the
**Fader** to about 0. **Too hot** shows what the fader can't fix. **Feedback** turns the monitor up with the wedge in
front of the mic (keep your volume low); the two **Fixed** presets show the two cures: the mic's dead side toward
the wedge, or a narrow cut at the frequency that rings.

## Sound check

1. Everything on in the right order ([Gear 1](gear-power.qmd)), master down.
2. One channel at a time: gain, then fader.
3. Monitors: ask each player what they need more of. Their voice/instrument first.
4. The whole band: balance from the audience, not from behind the mixer if you can help it.
5. Leave headroom. A crowd absorbs sound, and everyone plays louder at the gig.

## Feedback

The howl or squeal when a mic hears a speaker that's playing that mic.

- Keep the **mains in front** of the mics, never behind.
- Point the mic's **dead side** at the monitor (the back of a cardioid; the sides at ~120° for a supercardioid).
- Sing **close** to the mic: then the gain can stay lower.
- Don't cup the mic's grille: it changes the pattern to omni and feeds back.
- If it rings, pull the **monitor** or that channel down first, then find the ringing frequency with EQ.

## Loudness and stage volume

The quietest stage that still works sounds best out front. Turn amps toward the players (tilt them back, or put them
on a stand) rather than turning them up. See also [Recording 7: Mono and Stereo](rec-stereo.qmd) for live speaker
placement and subwoofers.
